# Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two Measured Preconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement

De Wang Affiliation: Uniphore Email: [de.wang@uniphore.com](mailto:)   
Peng Qi Affiliation: Uniphore Email: [peng.qi@uniphore.com](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Agent platforms are starting to improve their own agents: they read a
deployed agent’s execution traces, derive a change, have an automated
verifier approve it, and release it with no human author. How much of
this loop can safely run without a human? We propose two quantities a
platform can measure. _Verifier strength_ $`\sigma`$ is how well the
available verifier — often an LLM judge — agrees with a trusted
reference verifier; it limits how much a step can improve the agent.
_Recoverability_ is how cheaply a bad change can be undone: whether
undoing it needs a new verifier approval, and how much of the old
behavior a rollback restores. A step should run unattended only if both
are adequate. On our platform this rule allows prompt, tool and skill
edits to run unattended and keeps weight updates under human sign-off.

Our main contribution is these two definitions and how to measure them.
We built a platform that applies the rule and tested it in two ways: on
the platform’s own approval gate, and in controlled experiments on the
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench agent benchmark. On verifier strength, the platform’s
LLM judge sometimes gave the same score no matter what it was shown (9
of 37 settings) and reported no error, so a verifier can look healthy
while approving anything; its strength must be measured, and two simple
tests catch the failure. On recoverability, restoring a saved copy
brought the agent back to its original behavior, but a regenerated undo
did not, so only changes whose old version is kept can be reversed
without a human; and while a change was deployed, it altered the outcome
of $`17\%`$ of tasks beyond normal run-to-run variation, which no undo
repairs. Together these support the rule: a change can run unattended
only when its old version is kept and its verifier’s strength has been
measured.

## 1 Introduction

Agents built on language models now hold conversations, call tools, and
write to business systems ([Yao et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Barres et
al., 2026](#bib.bib24)). They also fail often. On the $`\tau^{2}`$-bench
tasks we study the baseline agent solves just over half of its tasks,
through ordinary mistakes: a wrong tool call, a missing confirmation,
steps taken out of order ([Cuadron et al., 2026](#bib.bib25)). Fixing
such failures means reading traces, finding the cause, revising the
agent, checking the revision and deploying it. Done by hand, this does
not scale with the number of agents a platform hosts, so platforms have
begun to automate it ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib29); [Li & Zhu,
2026](#bib.bib27)).

We call one pass of this automated repair a _self-improvement step_: the
platform reads its own agents’ traces, derives a change, checks it with
a verifier and deploys it, with no person writing the change.
Inference-time self-correction ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib16);
[Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib15)) and human-written fixes do not count.
Training and serving became platform services long ago ([Baylor et al.,
2017](#bib.bib9); [Moritz et al., 2018](#bib.bib10)); this loop has not,
yet it needs the same things: a budget, controlled access to the
deployed agent, a point where changes are admitted, and an audit trail
(§[4](#S4 "4 The platform: enforcing the rule ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).

This paper asks how much of the loop may run without a human. Our answer
rests on two measurable quantities
(§[2](#S2 "2 Definitions ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
Verifier strength measures how far the verifier’s approvals can be
trusted: its agreement with a reference verifier on a scale from $`-1`$
to $`1`$, where $`1`$ is perfect agreement and a verifier that always
gives the same answer scores $`0`$. Recoverability measures how cheaply
a bad change is undone. It records whether undoing a change needs a new
verifier approval and how much of the old behavior actually returns. If
no copy of the old version was kept (for example, after fine-tuning a
model in place), the undo must pass the same verifier that just approved
the mistake. Each quantity guards against a different failure, so a loop
can be only as autonomous as the weaker one allows
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Contributions. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
We derive this rule
(§[3](#S3 "3 The autonomy rule ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
build a platform that enforces it
(§[4](#S4 "4 The platform: enforcing the rule ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
and test the assumptions it rests on
(§[5](#S5 "5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
first in a case study of our platform’s own admission gate and then in
controlled experiments on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench. We do not address
adversarial or misaligned agents, only the ordinary failure of admitting
a change that should have been rejected.

#### Contributions.

Our main contribution is a method: the two definitions, how to measure
them, and the rule they support. (i) Two measurable preconditions for
unattended changes, and a rule that refuses whenever either is
unmeasured
(§[2](#S2 "2 Definitions ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement"),
§[3](#S3 "3 The autonomy rule ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
(ii) A platform that enforces the rule by typing changes by
recoverability, declaring verifiers as resources, and recording refusal
as its own outcome
(§[4](#S4 "4 The platform: enforcing the rule ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
(iii) Tests of the rule’s assumptions: a case study of _silent gate
collapse_ in our platform’s own admission gate, with two tests that
catch it
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
and experiments that vary each quantity separately for prompt edits on
two $`\tau^{2}`$-bench domains
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
Our verdicts for tool, skill and weight changes follow from the
definitions and are not separately tested.

## 2 Definitions

We write an agent as $`A=(\theta,p,T,K)`$: model weights, system prompt,
tool schemas and skills.

#### Self-improvement step.

A change $`A\mapsto A^{\prime}`$ that the platform derives from $`A`$’s
own traces, in the spirit of self-taught training ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib13)), and admits through a verifier, with no human writing
it. _Running example:_ airline traces show the agent canceling bookings
without asking the user; the loop adds “confirm before any cancellation”
to $`p`$, an LLM judge approves the edit, and it goes live. We measure a
step by $`\Delta_{k}`$, the change in the share of held-out tasks solved
in _all_ $`k`$ repeated trials, because a platform cares about
reliability rather than best cases.

#### Recoverability.

For a change $`\iota`$ and its undo $`\iota^{-1}`$ we measure three
things. _Re-approval_ $`g(\iota)\in\{0,1\}`$ records whether the way
back from $`A^{\prime}`$ to $`A`$ needs a new verifier approval. If the
old value was kept, the undo is a plain write and $`g{=}0`$; this holds
for prompt and schema edits and for a retained model checkpoint. If no
old value was kept, as after fine-tuning from the current checkpoint,
the undo must itself be generated and approved, so $`g{=}1`$. Both other
measures use a fixed set of probe tasks $`P`$, scored pass or fail.
_Restoration fidelity_ $`\rho(\iota)`$ asks whether the undo brings the
old behavior back: it is the share of tasks in $`P`$ with the same
outcome after the change is undone as before the change was made. _Blast
radius_ $`\beta(\iota)`$ is the share of tasks in $`P`$ whose outcome
changed while $`\iota`$ was deployed, relative to the unchanged agent:
what even a perfect rollback cannot recover, because those outcomes were
already delivered. In our experiments
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
$`P`$ is the 20 held-out test tasks for $`\rho`$ (the 30 training tasks
for the regenerated undos) and all 50 airline tasks for $`\beta`$. The
agent and the simulated user are both stochastic, so we also run a _null
change_ (no change at all), which gives noise floors $`\rho_{0}<1`$ and
$`\beta_{0}>0`$; only values beyond these floors count. Because
$`\beta`$ covers only the probe tasks, it is a lower bound: real side
effects such as an issued refund must be tracked at the tool boundary,
where recent work locates recoverability for agents ([Yang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib30); [Zheng et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)).

#### Verifier strength.

A verifier scores a trajectory as pass or fail; it may be a program or
an LLM judge ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)). Given a trusted
reference verifier $`v^{\star}`$ and a set of trajectories $`C`$,
strength is the Matthews correlation
$`\sigma(v)=\mathrm{MCC}(v,v^{\star})\big|_{C}\in[-1,1]`$. We use MCC
rather than accuracy because a verifier that always gives the same
answer scores exactly $`\sigma{=}0`$, whereas its accuracy equals the
share of the more common verdict and can look respectable.

## 3 The autonomy rule

#### The rule.

A change may go live without human sign-off only if $`g(\iota){=}0`$ and
$`\sigma(v)\geq\sigma_{\min}`$, where $`\sigma_{\min}`$ reflects the
cost of wrongly admitting a bad change. If either quantity is
unmeasured, the platform refuses. Our data do not fix $`\sigma_{\min}`$:
the strength below which weak verifiers start to hurt moves by
$`\pm 0.15`$ with the number of simulations the gate averages, so a
threshold from one benchmark would not transfer
(App. [E](#A5 "Appendix E Choosing 𝜎_min and limiting false admits ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
gives the numbers and a calibration procedure). In the running example
the old prompt is kept, so $`g{=}0`$, and $`\sigma`$ is the judge’s
agreement with $`\tau^{2}`$-bench’s database check; the edit goes live
only if that $`\sigma`$ was measured and clears $`\sigma_{\min}`$. A
fine-tune with no checkpoint kept has $`g{=}1`$ and is refused however
good the judge is.

#### Why both conditions.

A self-improvement step does two things: it _decides_ whether to admit
$`A\to A^{\prime}`$, and then it _changes_ a live system. Each quantity
bounds one of these failures. Verifier strength bounds the decision,
because the verdict is the loop’s only evidence that $`A^{\prime}`$ is
better than $`A`$; at $`\sigma{=}0`$ the verdict says nothing about
quality ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)). Recoverability bounds the
change. At $`g{=}0`$ the platform writes back the old value and pays
only for the traffic served while the change was deployed, which is what
$`\beta`$ measures. At $`g{=}1`$ the old value is gone, so the way back
must be regenerated and approved by the same gate that made the mistake.
Neither quantity can make up for the other, so autonomy is limited by
the weaker one rather than traded between them. A strong verifier cannot
justify an irreversible change, since its errors would then be
permanent, and easy rollback cannot justify a weak verifier, since the
loop would only churn the agent.

#### Assumptions to test.

The rule rests on three assumptions, which
§[5](#S5 "5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
tests: (a) a verifier’s strength cannot be taken for granted and must be
measured; (b) a weaker verifier admits worse changes; and (c) keeping
the old value makes rollback exact and losing it does not, while an
admitted change still affects tasks that rollback cannot undo.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: The rule as a matrix, with our platform’s intervention types
placed. A change runs unattended only when both preconditions hold
(shaded); every other cell needs a human.

## 4 The platform: enforcing the rule

#### What the platform does.

Our platform improves deployed agents from their own production traces.
For each agent it (1) collects execution traces and classifies failures,
such as a wrong tool sequence, outdated knowledge or a degraded prompt;
(2) maps each failure to a change along one of four dimensions:
rewriting the system prompt, fixing a tool definition, updating a skill,
or fine-tuning a small model on distilled traces; (3) builds the
candidate and evaluates it; and (4) promotes it or stops. Each attempt
runs as a recorded session, so every deployed change can be traced back
to the evidence that admitted it, as in production ML pipelines ([Baylor
et al., 2017](#bib.bib9)). We built this loop to enforce the rule; three
design choices put the rule into it.

#### Changes are typed by recoverability.

An agent can be changed in four ways — weights, system prompt, tool
definitions and skills — and each is a separate resource type that
records how it is undone and hence its $`g`$
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C Recoverability in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
This lets “may this proceed without a human?” have a different answer
for each type
(Figure [2](#S3.F2.fig1 "Figure 2 ‣ Assumptions to test. ‣ 3 The autonomy rule ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
Prompt, tool-schema and skill edits are undone by a write and may
promote automatically. Weight updates can be undone by re-pinning the
previous adapter, but their verifier is a learned judge of the kind
§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
shows can fail silently, so they need human sign-off. A training-data
filter with no workable verifier ships disabled.

#### Evaluation decides what goes live.

A proposed change is not deployed until evaluation approves it, so
evaluation works like an admission check in other
platforms ([Kubernetes, 2026](#bib.bib26)): if it fails or cannot run,
nothing is deployed; every decision is logged; and no caller can skip
it. Each agent declares which verifiers it uses, with each verifier’s
measured $`\sigma`$, so before promoting a change the platform can check
whether an adequate verifier exists.

#### Refusal is a recorded decision.

The rule has three outcomes, not two: admit, reject (the change is
worse), and refuse (the platform cannot decide unattended because
$`\sigma`$ is unmeasured or the old value is gone). Ours records each
refusal with the missing precondition, so a human sees what is waiting
and why instead of a change that silently waits forever.

## 5 Experiments and results

We test the three assumptions in two settings: a case study of our
platform’s own admission gate
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
and controlled experiments on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Admitted changes reach tasks that rollback cannot undo (B). ‣ 5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
summarizes what each result implies.

### 5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform

This case study tests assumption (a), that a verifier’s strength must be
measured rather than assumed. Before our platform fine-tunes a model, it
collects agent traces into a training set, and an LLM-judge gate scores
the set’s diversity; a set that scores too low is not used for training.
This gate is a verifier in the sense of
§[2](#S2 "2 Definitions ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement"):
it decides whether a change, here a weight update, may proceed. It had
been treated as working because it always returned a score. (A second
gate, which filters individual training rows, ships disabled;
App. [A](#A1 "Appendix A The gate case study in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement").)

#### A diversity gate that ignores half its instructions.

The gate’s LLM judge ([Zheng et al., 2023](#bib.bib17)) scores the
training set from 0 to 1. Its prompt asks for two things: reward
_breadth_ (many distinct seed tasks) and penalize _imbalance_ (a few
seeds dominating); the input gives the imbalance as a number. We tested
3 judge models, 4 prompt variants, 4 imbalance levels, breadths 3–12 and
two agent configurations: 172 settings of 10 runs each. In the deployed
setting the gate ignores imbalance completely. It returned 0.250 in all
40 runs with zero spread, exactly what it returns when every mention of
imbalance is removed from the prompt. This is not an artifact of greedy
decoding, since 98 of the 172 settings vary. Full collapse, the same
score at all four imbalance levels, occurs in 9 of 37 configurations,
all on the deployed judge, the smallest of the three. That judge also
ran most configurations (33 of 37), so the count alone does not
implicate it; a matched comparison does: on identical inputs the
deployed judge stays flat while both larger judges track imbalance
($`p<10^{-11}`$ each;
App. [A](#A1 "Appendix A The gate case study in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).

_Implication._ We call this _silent gate collapse_: a gate sound in one
configuration and empty in another, with no error to show the
difference. A constant score looks like a confident answer; this is the
$`\sigma{=}0`$ point of
§[2](#S2 "2 Definitions ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement"),
and it supports assumption (a).

Two cheap tests catch this, each costing a handful of calls, and both
belong in the platform. Delete the signal: remove the property the gate
claims to measure and check that its score changes. Check the
guarantees: verify that request-level settings the gate relies on
actually took effect; three of ours did not, forced tool calls among
them
(App. [B](#A2 "Appendix B The two acceptance tests ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
What did work was stating the criterion as a checkable bound: “if the
largest seed exceeds 50%, score at most 0.10” held in all 16 settings
above 50%, where the original wording never scored that low (30 of 30
runs vs. 0 of 30 on matched inputs, Fisher $`p<10^{-16}`$;
Table [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Setup. ‣ Appendix A The gate case study in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).

### 5.2 Controlled experiments on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench

Assumptions (b) and (c) need controlled conditions, since on a live
platform the two quantities change together. We fix one and vary the
other: experiment A tests (b), experiment B tests (c). Both use
$`\tau^{2}`$-bench, whose agents match ours (multi-turn, tool-using,
database-backed, with a simulated user) and whose task score is the
product of a configurable subset of five checks ([Barres et al.,
2026](#bib.bib24)). Changing the subset changes the verifier $`v`$ while
leaving tasks, agent and environment fixed, and scoring is separate from
running, so one set of trajectories can be re-scored under every
verifier.

#### Setup.

We use the airline domain: 50 tasks split 30 for training and 20 for
testing, with natural-language assertions on every task, so a program
verifier and an LLM judge score the _same_ trajectories, the comparison
§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
could not make in production. The reference verifier combines
database-state equality with communication checks; the latter apply to
only 4 of 80 test trajectories, so on the other 76 the reference is
database equality alone. The loop is ours, reduced to one recipe: read
failed training trajectories, propose a system-prompt revision, admit it
if the verifier under test prefers it, and measure the result on the
test split with the reference verifier. We report mean pass rate rather
than $`\mathrm{pass}^{k}`$, which at four trials discards partial
credit. A1 measures $`\sigma`$ for real verifiers; A2 tests whether
lower $`\sigma`$ picks worse changes; B fixes the verifier at the
reference and compares restoring a stored copy ($`g{=}0`$) with
regenerating the undo ($`g{=}1`$). Weight updates are not tested. Each
agent is run twice per training task and four times per test task.
Intervals are $`95\%`$ task-resampling bootstrap intervals
(App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Experiment A in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
paired for differences ([Miller, 2024](#bib.bib20)). Where the
hypothesis fixes a direction we report one-sided $`p`$-values, and we
correct across candidates with Holm’s method.

#### Real verifiers (A1).

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Real verifiers (A1). ‣ 5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
gives $`\sigma`$ for each verifier on one set of 80 test trajectories
(20 tasks, 4 trials each). The LLM judge reaches $`\sigma{=}0.70`$
against the program check on the _same_ trajectories, far above zero
(Fisher $`p<10^{-9}`$) but far from perfect. Its errors are clustered:
all 4 false admits come from one task and the 8 false rejects from two,
repeated across trials, so resampling whole tasks widens its interval to
$`[0.36,1.00]`$. A verifier that approves everything scores exactly
$`0`$ while passing all 42 failing trajectories.

#### Weaker verifiers pick worse changes, but not significantly (A2).

To get a fine-grained $`\sigma`$ scale cheaply, we flip each reference
verdict with probability $`\varepsilon`$, which gives a verifier of
known strength; re-scoring one set of trajectories yields every point,
each averaged over 400 random draws. _Regret_, how much worse the picked
change is than the one a perfect verifier would pick, rises from
$`0.000`$ at $`\sigma{=}1`$ to $`0.067`$ at $`\sigma{\approx}0`$
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Real verifiers (A1). ‣ 5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")),
as predicted, but the fitted slope ($`-0.065`$, CI $`[-0.234,0.120]`$)
includes zero (one-sided $`p{=}0.23`$); resolving it would take about
220 held-out tasks, eleven times our 20. The bottleneck is the
candidates, not $`\sigma`$: the candidate a perfect verifier would pick
is only $`0.069`$ above the average one, so even a random pick loses
little, and the observed $`0.067`$ is already $`98\%`$ of that maximum
(App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Experiment A in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).
Retail shows no trend (slope $`+0.008`$, CI $`[-0.115,0.109]`$), but its
candidates are so similar that replication is untested rather than
failed.

#### Two secondary observations (A).

With a perfect verifier the loop still overstated its own gain
($`0.20`$; one-sided $`p{=}0.08`$, not in retail), and two verifiers
with nearly equal $`\sigma`$ erred in opposite directions
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Real verifiers (A1). ‣ 5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement");
App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Experiment A in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement"), [E](#A5 "Appendix E Choosing 𝜎_min and limiting false admits ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).

#### Only a stored copy restores behavior (B).

With the verifier fixed at the reference, a null change sets the noise
floors ($`\rho_{0}{=}0.95`$, CI $`[0.89,1.00]`$; $`\beta_{0}{=}0.08`$,
CI $`[0.02,0.16]`$). Restoring a prompt edit from a stored copy
($`g{=}0`$) returns behavior to the floor: $`\rho-\rho_{0}{=}0.000`$ (CI
$`[-0.038,0.038]`$), equivalent to zero within $`\pm 0.05`$ (TOST
$`p{=}0.007`$). Without a stored copy ($`g{=}1`$) the undo must be
regenerated, and three regenerated undos left behavior measurably
different from the baseline: $`\rho-\rho_{0}{=}{-}0.16`$ (CI
$`[-0.27,-0.07]`$, one-sided $`p{=}0.0001`$; each undo significant after
Holm correction), measured on the training split against a floor of
$`0.98`$. The gate refused all three, as the rule requires
(App. [C](#A3 "Appendix C Recoverability in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).

#### Admitted changes reach tasks that rollback cannot undo (B).

Deployed on all 50 probe tasks, the three admitted changes with complete
data altered the outcome of $`17\%`$ of tasks beyond the noise floor
($`\beta-\beta_{0}{=}0.17`$, CI $`[0.08,0.27]`$, one-sided
$`p{=}0.0002`$), and each change does so on its own after Holm
correction. Tasks flipped in both directions in nearly equal numbers (18
up, 20 down), so the average effect is near zero while the reach is not,
and reach is what rollback cannot undo ([Garcia-Molina & Salem,
1987](#bib.bib1)).

| Precondition      | Finding                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     | Implication for unattended changes                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Verifier strength | Platform’s LLM gate gave a constant in 9/37 settings, no error (§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")) | A gate can look healthy while approving anything: measure $`\sigma`$                                                                                                                                                            |
| Verifier strength | Weaker verifiers picked worse changes; not significant at 20 tasks (A2)                                                                                                                                                                                                     | $`\sigma_{\min}`$ must be calibrated per platform (App. [E](#A5 "Appendix E Choosing 𝜎_min and limiting false admits ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")) |
| Recoverability    | Saved copy restores exactly; regenerated undo does not (B)                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | Only changes with $`g{=}0`$ can be undone without a human                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Recoverability    | A deployed change altered $`17\%`$ of tasks beyond noise (B)                                                                                                                                                                                                                | Undoing a change does not repair what it already did                                                                                                                                                                            |

Table 3: Each result, the precondition it tests, and what it implies for
unattended self-improvement.

## 6 Related work and discussion

Production ML platforms made training and serving platform
services ([Baylor et al., 2017](#bib.bib9); [Breck et al.,
2019](#bib.bib11); [Moritz et al., 2018](#bib.bib10); [Sculley et al.,
2015](#bib.bib5)), but not deciding what to change in a deployed agent.
Self-improvement and prompt-optimization methods ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib16); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib15); [Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib13); [Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)) supply the
changes we schedule but assume a trustworthy verifier; work on reward
gaming and LLM judges questions that assumption ([Skalse et al.,
2022](#bib.bib12); [Gao et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Zheng et al.,
2023](#bib.bib17)), and verifiable-reward methods avoid it ([Lambert et
al., 2025](#bib.bib22); [Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2026](#bib.bib28)).
Deployment engineering gates changes on measured evidence ([Humble &
Farley, 2010](#bib.bib3); [Beyer et al., 2016](#bib.bib7); [Kubernetes,
2026](#bib.bib26)) but assumes a human author. Closest is off-policy
evaluation, which promotes only when a lower confidence bound beats the
incumbent ([Thomas et al., 2015](#bib.bib6); [Thomas & Brunskill,
2016](#bib.bib8); [Sakhi et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)); $`\sigma`$ plays
that role where no unbiased value estimate exists.

#### Limitations.

The rule comes from one platform and was applied after the fact; only
prompt edits were tested end to end, on $`\tau^{2}`$-bench airline and
retail rather than in production; and experiment A was too small to
confirm the $`\sigma`$ effect
(App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Experiment A in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")).

#### Conclusion.

A self-improvement loop may run without a human only where the old
version is kept and the verifier’s strength is measured; where either is
missing, the platform should refuse.

## Appendix A The gate case study in detail

#### Setup.

A training set is built from a few _seed tasks_; the number of distinct
seed tasks is its _breadth_, and the share of examples coming from the
most common seed task is its _imbalance_. We sent the production
diversity gate, with its production prompt, training sets whose
imbalance we set by hand, holding everything else fixed (number and
quality of examples, agent, task list). Each setting was run 10 times.
The runs came in five batches
(Table [5](#A1.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Setup. ‣ Appendix A The gate case study in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")):
172 settings and 1,720 calls, of which 1,718 returned a score (the two
others answered in plain text when the scoring tool was offered but not
required). The script and data are available from the authors on
request.

|           |           |                    |       |       |         |                     |
| --------- | --------- | ------------------ | ----- | ----- | ------- | ------------------- |
|           |           | largest-seed share |       |       |         |                     |
|           |           | .33/.17            | .50   | .67   | .83/.79 | $`r_{s}`$           |
| breadth 3 | deployed  | 0.250              | 0.250 | 0.250 | 0.250   | —                   |
|           | no-signal | 0.250              | 0.250 | 0.250 | 0.250   | —                   |
|           | threshold | 0.250              | 0.100 | 0.100 | 0.090   | $`-0.845`$          |
| breadth 6 | deployed  | 0.938              | 0.506 | 0.445 | 0.371   | $`\mathbf{-0.836}`$ |
|           | no-signal | 0.842              | 0.803 | 0.891 | 0.832   | $`+0.063`$          |
|           | threshold | 0.919              | 0.100 | 0.098 | 0.094   | $`-0.786`$          |

Table 4: Scores from the diversity gate on the four-tool agent. Each
column is an imbalance level: the share of training examples that come
from the most common seed task (the lowest possible share is .33 with 3
seed tasks and .17 with 6). Each cell averages 10 runs. no-signal
removes all imbalance information from the prompt, so it cannot respond
to imbalance; threshold states the rule as a number. $`r_{s}`$ is the
rank correlation between score and imbalance (— when the score never
changes).

| batch | what varies                                                      | settings | calls |
| ----- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | -------- | ----- |
| A     | imbalance $`\times`$ judge model, breadth 3 and 6                | 24       | 240   |
| B     | imbalance $`\times`$ prompt variant, breadth 3 and 6             | 32       | 320   |
| C     | imbalance $`\times`$ how the score is requested                  | 24       | 238   |
| R     | repeat of one dataset pair                                       | 24       | 240   |
| S     | imbalance $`\times`$ breadth $`\in\{3,4,5,6,8,12\}`$, two agents | 68       | 680   |
|       | total                                                            | 172      | 1,718 |

Table 5: The five batches of runs. The judge models are claude-haiku-4-5
(used in production), claude-sonnet-5 and claude-opus-5. The prompt
variants are shipped (production), stat-only (the imbalance instruction
deleted, the number kept), threshold and no-signal.

#### The collapse is real.

The judge models do not let us set the sampling temperature, so every
call used the provider’s default. Scores vary from run to run in 98 of
the 172 settings, so a score that never changes is not explained by
deterministic decoding. We call a configuration _collapsed_ when it
gives the same score at all four imbalance levels. Nine of 37
configurations collapsed, all with the production judge. That judge was
also used in 33 of the 37 configurations, so this count on its own is
not significant (Fisher exact test, $`p{=}0.55`$). The stronger evidence
is batch A, which gives all three judges identical inputs: at breadth 3
the production judge returns the same score at every imbalance level,
while both larger judges change their score with imbalance
($`p<10^{-11}`$ each). Collapse also depends on the agent: the six-tool
agent tracks imbalance perfectly at breadth 3 but collapses at breadths
4, 5 and 8.

#### The fix works.

With the threshold wording, the gate scored at most 0.10 in all 16
settings where the most common seed task supplies more than half of the
examples. On identical inputs this happened in 30 of 30 runs, against 0
of 30 with the original wording (Fisher exact test, $`p<10^{-16}`$).

#### The second gate.

A second gate removes low-scoring rows from training data. It ships
switched off, because a safe threshold turned out to differ from agent
to agent, and keeping unscored rows stops an unreliable judge from
quietly shrinking the training set.

## Appendix B The two acceptance tests

#### Test 1: delete the signal.

Copy the gate’s real input and remove the property it is supposed to
judge, entirely rather than setting it to a neutral value, so the prompt
reads the same whatever the property’s value (the no-signal variant
above). Run both versions the same number of times. If the scores are
the same, the gate is ignoring the property. Ours took 40 calls. Repeat
the test whenever the model, the prompt or the request format changes,
because
§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Case study: silent gate collapse in our platform ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
shows a gate can work in one setup and fail in another.

#### Test 2: check the guarantees.

List the request settings the gate depends on, such as requiring a tool
call, requiring a fixed output format, or setting the temperature. For
each one, send an input that would be answered differently if the
setting were ignored, and check that the answer changes. Three of ours
failed. Requiring a tool call cannot be combined with extended
reasoning: the API rejects the request. Our company’s gateway forwarded
requests for a fixed output format _without_ the format, and said
nothing. And the judge models reject temperature settings. We measured
these on 2026-08-13 with one provider through one gateway; both change
over time, so each setting must be tested, not taken from documentation.

## Appendix C Recoverability in detail

| dimension        | how it is undone          | $`g`$ | are its side effects undone? |
| ---------------- | ------------------------- | ----- | ---------------------------- |
| system prompt    | write back previous value | 0     | no: answers already served   |
| tool definitions | write back previous value | 0     | no: calls already made       |
| skills           | write back previous value | 0     | no: answers already served   |
| model weights    | re-pin previous adapter   | 0     | no: answers already served   |

Table 6: How each type of change is undone on our platform. All four
keep the old version, so undoing is a write and $`g{=}0`$ (for weights,
switching back to the previous adapter). None of them can take back what
the change already did to users.

#### Noise floors.

The agent and the simulated user are both stochastic, so running the
_same_ agent twice already changes some outcomes. We measure this by
running the unchanged agent twice (the null change). Its restoration
fidelity is $`\rho_{0}{=}0.95`$ (CI $`[0.89,1.00]`$) on the 20 test
tasks, and its blast radius is $`\beta_{0}{=}0.08`$ (CI $`[0.02,0.16]`$)
on all 50 airline tasks with four runs per task. We first used 20 tasks
for blast radius, but the floor was too noisy, so we moved to 50; more
tasks helped, more runs per task did not.

#### Restoring a saved copy ($`g{=}0`$).

Writing back the saved prompt gives $`\rho{=}0.95`$, so
$`\rho-\rho_{0}{=}0.000`$ (CI $`[-0.038,0.038]`$). An equivalence test
(TOST) with a margin of $`\pm 0.05`$, one task in 20, confirms that the
restored agent behaves like the original ($`p{=}0.007`$). Three separate
runs of the original agent agree with each other no more closely
($`\rho`$ of 0.950, 0.950 and 0.975). This is the expected result, since
the restored prompt is identical, but it is the control the other
comparisons rely on.

#### Regenerating the undo ($`g{=}1`$).

Here we hid the old prompt, as when a fine-tuned model’s previous
version is gone, and asked the optimizer to write an undo. It wrote
three. We compared each with the original agent on the 30 training
tasks, against a floor measured with the same two runs per task
($`\rho_{0}{=}0.98`$). The three undos reach $`\rho`$ of 0.75, 0.83 and
0.90, that is, 0.23, 0.15 and 0.08 below the floor (one-sided
$`p{=}0.0005`$, 0.004 and 0.04, all still significant after Holm’s
correction for testing three); together, 0.16 below (CI $`[0.07,0.27]`$,
$`p{=}0.0001`$). So a regenerated undo does not bring the original
behavior back, while a saved copy does; the two differ by about 0.16.
Three caveats: these runs use the training tasks, not the test tasks
used for the saved copy; the gate refused all three undos, so this shows
what would have happened had one been installed; and the three are close
rewrites of one another, so they test one kind of undo rather than many.
The gate refused them because their training pass rates (0.567, 0.517,
0.517) were below the original’s (0.617), though that gap is too small
to be significant ($`-0.05`$, CI $`[-0.23,0.13]`$).

#### Blast radius.

We deployed four admitted changes, one at a time, in place of the
original agent and ran each on the 50 tasks. One change’s test runs were
lost, so we report the other three: blast radius 0.24, 0.28 and 0.24,
against the 0.08 floor. Together they exceed the floor by 0.17 (CI
$`[0.08,0.27]`$, one-sided $`p{=}0.0002`$; a permutation test and a
Wilcoxon test agree), and each change does on its own (exact McNemar
tests, $`p{=}0.029`$, 0.003 and 0.019; at most 0.04 after Holm’s
correction). Tasks flipped from pass to fail about as often as from fail
to pass (20 and 18), so the average pass rate barely moved even though
about one task in six changed outcome.

## Appendix D Experiment A in detail

#### Why 20 test tasks are too few.

A task’s outcome is close to all-or-nothing: its four runs usually
agree, and the same task often flips completely between one candidate
and another. So differences between candidates are mostly whole tasks,
and with 20 test tasks the uncertainty on a candidate’s test score is
about $`\pm 0.24`$. Confirming the regret trend would take about 220
test tasks, and confirming the overstated gain about 60.

#### Intervals.

All intervals come from resampling tasks with replacement: 2,000
resamples in experiment A and 20,000 elsewhere.

#### How the regret slope is fit.

For each corruption level $`\varepsilon`$ from 0 to 0.5 in steps of 0.05
(Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Real verifiers (A1). ‣ 5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement")
shows every other level), we measure $`\sigma`$ and the regret, each
averaged over 400 random corruptions. The slope is a straight-line
(least-squares) fit of regret against $`\sigma`$ through these 11
points; a negative slope means regret grows as the verifier gets weaker.
For its interval we resample the training and test tasks 2,000 times and
refit the whole curve each time; the one-sided $`p`$-value is the share
of refitted slopes that are zero or positive.

#### When can a candidate pool show the effect at all?

A verifier with $`\sigma{=}0`$ picks a candidate at random, so the most
it can lose is the gap between the average candidate and the one a
perfect verifier would pick. If that gap is smaller than the measurement
noise, no experiment on this pool can show the effect; we call such a
pool _field-limited_, and we fixed the threshold (gap divided by noise
below 1) in advance. Airline’s gap is 0.069, a ratio of 0.62, and
retail’s is negative ($`-0.009`$), so both pools are field-limited. Our
first version of this check used a rougher estimate that put airline at
1.39; we corrected it after the runs. We do not combine domains, because
the pools with the least spread also have the smallest error bars and
would dominate a combined estimate.

#### Widening the pool.

The loop’s own four revisions gave a ratio of at most 0.42, so we added
candidates made by deleting one section of the agent’s instructions
(no-cancel, no-book, no-modify, and two pairs of these), each keeping at
least 60% of the instructions so that it is weakened rather than broken.
One candidate’s test runs were lost, leaving eight, with test pass rates
from 0.26 to 0.60.

#### The overstated gain.

The 0.20 gap at $`\varepsilon{=}0`$ has two parts: a difference between
the training and test tasks that affects every candidate (0.09, CI
$`[-0.09,0.26]`$, one-sided $`p{=}0.17`$), and the extra gain of the
candidate that was picked because it scored best on training, known as
the winner’s curse (0.11, CI $`[-0.08,0.33]`$, $`p{=}0.13`$). Neither
part is significant, and neither is the total ($`p{=}0.08`$). In retail
the gap is $`-0.02`$ (CI $`[-0.18,0.18]`$), so it does not replicate.

#### Data checks.

A simulation that fails because of an infrastructure error still takes
its place in the results, with an empty transcript and no score, and the
benchmark runner reports no error. We therefore checked every set of
runs before scoring and only compared runs with the same number of runs
per task.

## Appendix E Choosing $`\sigma_{\min}`$ and limiting false admits

#### How to set $`\sigma_{\min}`$.

(i) Decide how much regret $`r`$ the domain can tolerate, from the cost
of admitting a bad change. (ii) Build a candidate pool that is not
field-limited
(App. [D](#A4 "Appendix D Experiment A in detail ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement"));
if that is not possible, no threshold can be estimated. (iii) Measure
regret against $`\sigma`$ as in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Real verifiers (A1). ‣ 5.2 Controlled experiments on 𝜏^2-bench ‣ 5 Experiments and results ‣ Recoverability and Verifier Strength: Two MeasuredPreconditions for Unattended Agent Self-Improvement"),
and set $`\sigma_{\min}`$ to the smallest $`\sigma`$ at which the
_upper_ end of the confidence interval on regret is at most $`r`$.
(iv) Repeat whenever the number of runs the gate averages over changes:
the strength at which regret starts to rise was 0.41 with 60 runs per
candidate, 0.56 with 30 and 0.49 with 15.

#### Limit false admits, not only $`\sigma`$.

Let $`\alpha`$ be the false-admit rate (how often the verifier passes a
trajectory the reference fails) and $`\varphi`$ the false-reject rate.
Our LLM judge has $`(\alpha,\varphi){=}(0.10,0.21)`$ and
reference-action match $`(0.21,0.12)`$: almost the same $`\sigma`$ but
opposite mistakes, although with 20 tasks the difference is not
significant. Only false admits let a worse change through, so where
those are costly the rule should also require the upper confidence bound
on $`\alpha`$ to stay below a limit $`\alpha_{\max}`$, with $`\sigma>0`$
to rule out collapse. Because mistakes repeat across a task’s runs, the
bound must count tasks rather than runs: the judge’s 4 false admits are
one task seen four times, which puts the upper bound near 0.37, not the
0.20 that counting runs suggests. Showing $`\alpha\leq 0.05`$ with no
false admits at all takes about 59 separate tasks that the reference
fails.

#### Keeping $`\sigma`$ up to date.

$`\sigma`$ belongs to a verifier _together with_ its model and settings,
since the same gate collapsed in some setups and not others. A
$`\sigma`$ measured before such a change counts as unmeasured, so the
rule refuses. The reference does not have to be a program, only fixed:
label a balanced set of trajectories once and re-score that same set
each time. Where no program check exists, one can be learned from
labeled examples ([Pezeshkpour & Hruschka, 2026](#bib.bib28)), but it
must then be measured on examples it was not learned from.

#### Correcting the overstated gain.

The winner’s-curse part can be removed by promoting a candidate on the
lower end of its confidence interval rather than on its best training
score ([Thomas et al., 2015](#bib.bib6); [Thomas & Brunskill,
2016](#bib.bib8); [Sakhi et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)), or reduced with
statistical corrections for selecting the best of several ([Andrews et
al., 2024](#bib.bib18); [Efron, 2011](#bib.bib4); [Zöllner & Pritchard,
2007](#bib.bib2)). The part that affects every candidate needs a set of
test tasks the gate never uses for selection. We recommend both; we have
not yet compared them on our data.
